# MEMORANDUM

**TO:** Supervising Partner
**FROM:** [Associate]
**DATE:** November 18, 2026
**RE:** Treikaith Interactive, Inc. / Daibaind Games, LLC: Emberfall Saga asset purchase, buyer-side issues list

**PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL | ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

---

## I. Executive Summary

Treikaith Interactive, Inc. ("**Treikaith**") signed an Asset Purchase Agreement (the "**APA**") with Daibaind Games, LLC ("**Daibaind**") on September 15, 2026. It is buying the Emberfall Saga franchise business for a **Purchase Price of $48,000,000** (APA §2.2). Of that amount, $4,800,000 goes into indemnity escrow with Pellmont Trust Company, N.A. (APA §2.3).

The general indemnity **Cap is 10% of the Purchase Price ($4,800,000)** (APA §9.5(a)). The APA is governed by Delaware law, with exclusive jurisdiction in the Delaware Court of Chancery (§§11.6, 11.7). Closing has not occurred. Either party may terminate if Closing has not happened by **December 31, 2026** (§8.1(b)).

I reviewed all eight documents in the folder. I found six substantive issues. Several appear only when two documents are read together. Taken together, they materially weaken the protection Treikaith thinks it bargained for.

### Items needing your immediate attention

| # | Issue | Why it is urgent |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | The October 21 Side Letter removed the uncapped indemnity for Excluded Liabilities, including the loot-box class action. | We signed this as Buyer, and it controls over the APA. Seller's indemnity for the nationwide *Calloway* class action is now capped at $4.8M. |
| **2** | The Orvenna soundtrack objection was late. | Seller is already asserting deemed acceptance. Orvenna's 30-day injunction deadline (from September 28) has passed. The soundtrack sits in every shipped title. |
| **3** | The Kestrune engine consent is not a closing condition. | Assignment without consent is void, and every title runs on this engine. This must be fixed before Closing, and Closing could come within weeks. |
| **4** | The Key Employee Agreement uses California law. | The agreement is still unsigned, so it is easy to fix now and very hard to fix after Closing. |

Issues 5 (the escrow survival gap) and 6 (the title rep scope) are equally significant economically. They are less time-sensitive only because they can still be negotiated into the closing-form Escrow Agreement and an APA amendment. They should go in the same mark-up.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: The Side Letter drops the Excluded Liabilities carve-out from the Cap (HIGH PRIORITY)

**Where it appears**
- APA §9.5(a)–(b)
- APA §§9.2(c), 9.6, 11.9, 11.10
- Side Letter dated October 21, 2026, §§1.2(a), 2.1, 4.1
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 2.4, Item 1

**What the documents say**
- **Original APA §9.5(b).** The Cap and the threshold did not apply to Losses from:
  - (i) Fraud;
  - (ii) breach of Fundamental Representations; and
  - (iii) "Seller's obligations in respect of Excluded Liabilities pursuant to Section 9.2(c)."
- **Side Letter §2.1.** States that §9.5(b) "is hereby amended and restated in its entirety." The restated text carves out only "Fraud or breach of any Fundamental Representation." Clause (iii) is gone.
- **Side Letter §1.2(a).** Describes the change as a "conforming clarification."
- **Side Letter §4.1.** States that the Side Letter is an amendment executed under APA §11.9.
- **APA §11.10.** An amendment executed under §11.9 "controls over this Agreement."
- **Schedule 2.4, Item 1.** Lists *Calloway, et al. v. Daibaind Games, LLC* (W.D. Tex. No. 1:26-cv-00814) as an Excluded Liability. This is the putative nationwide class action over the "Ember Cache" randomized purchase mechanics, defined as the "Pre-Closing Player Litigation."

**Why it matters for Treikaith**
- Seller's indemnity for all Excluded Liabilities now sits under the $4,800,000 Cap (APA §9.5(a), which caps "all Losses under Section 9.2"). That includes:
  - the Pre-Closing Player Litigation;
  - pre-Closing taxes;
  - pre-Closing employee liabilities; and
  - any other pre-Closing operating liability.
- The Cap is also shared with every General Representation claim and every covenant claim. A large class settlement or judgment could use up the whole Cap.
- APA §9.6 still allows recovery directly from Seller for §9.2(c) claims. That right is now limited by the Cap, so it adds little.
- Exposure to the class action is real even in an asset deal:
  - Plaintiffs may pursue successor-liability theories against Treikaith as the new publisher of the same titles.
  - Treikaith may face injunctive-relief demands directed at the live games it will operate.
  - Texas AG interest in odds disclosures (Schedule 4.7, Item 2) increases the risk.
- This is not a "conforming clarification." It is a substantive concession. Nothing in the Side Letter, read alone, flags that a carve-out was deleted.
- Treikaith countersigned the Side Letter, so we cannot rely on the APA §11.10 precedence clause or on the original text.

**Recommended fix**
1. Before anything else goes back to the other side, confirm with the client whether the Side Letter has been fully executed. The copy in the folder has blank signature blocks but is styled "Agreed and accepted as of October 21, 2026."
2. Prepare Amendment No. 2 under APA §11.9 (signed by both parties and stating it is an amendment) restoring clause (iii). Suggested language: "(iii) Seller's obligations in respect of Excluded Liabilities pursuant to Section 9.2(c), including the Pre-Closing Player Litigation."
3. Consider adding stronger protection, either:
   - a stand-alone special indemnity for the Pre-Closing Player Litigation, uncapped, with no threshold and outside the escrow-only limit; or
   - a separate special escrow or holdback sized to the class exposure.
4. If Seller resists, our position is that the October 21 change was described as conforming and that clause (iii) was never intended to be dropped. A mutual-mistake or reformation argument is a fallback only. We should fix this by agreement.

---

### Issue 2: The objection to Supplement No. 1 was late, putting the Orvenna claim at risk of being "deemed cured" (HIGH PRIORITY)

**Where it appears**
- Disclosure Schedule, Part 3, Supplement No. 1, ¶¶4.1–4.4
- APA §6.3(b)
- APA §1.1 ("Business Day")
- APA §7.2(a)
- Side Letter §§1.2(b)–(d) and 3

**What the documents say**
- **APA §6.3(b).** Buyer must object in writing "within five (5) Business Days after receipt." Otherwise the Schedule Supplement "is deemed accepted by Buyer" and is "treated as having cured any inaccuracy in or breach of any representation or warranty disclosed in it." This applies both for Article IX indemnity and for the §7.2(a) bring-down condition.
- **Supplement No. 1 ¶4.1.** States it was "delivered to Buyer on October 2, 2026," a Friday, by email to Buyer's General Counsel, with an overnight courier copy.
- **Deadline calculation.** The five Business Days are Monday October 5 through Friday October 9, 2026. The window closed on **October 9, 2026**. That is before Columbus Day (October 12), so the bank-holiday definition does not extend it.
- **Side Letter recitals.** Buyer objected on **October 16, 2026**, one week late. Seller "contends that Supplement No. 1 was deemed accepted." Both parties reserve rights (Side Letter §§1.2(d), 3).

**What Supplement No. 1 discloses**
- Orvenna Sound Collective claims copyright ownership of compositions and sound recordings in the Emberfall Saga soundtrack, including the main theme and the in-game combat suite.
- It alleges infringement by the titles.
- It demands that distribution stop, plus an accounting and a revenue share.
- It threatens preliminary and permanent injunctive relief if not satisfied within 30 days of the September 28, 2026 letter. That date, about October 28, has passed.

**Why it matters for Treikaith**
- If deemed acceptance stands, Seller will argue that:
  - Treikaith has no indemnity claim for the Orvenna matter under Article IX, whether under §4.7 (Litigation), §4.9 (Material Contracts), §4.12(c) (non-infringement) or otherwise; and
  - the matter cannot be used to fail the §7.2(a) bring-down condition. Treikaith would then have to close over a live copyright claim against music in every shipped title.
- Treikaith's counter-arguments are weak:
  - Delivery by email to General Counsel is a permitted notice method (APA §11.2), and the courier copy only confirms it.
  - The best counter-argument is narrower. The Orvenna claim goes partly to title to the score (Schedule 4.9, Item 8 says Seller owns the score as a work made for hire). Title could be framed as a Fundamental Representation issue. But APA §4.12(a) title covers only "Assigned IP" (see Issue 6), so that argument is also thin.
  - The Side Letter's reservation of rights preserves the dispute. It does not resolve it in our favor.
- An injunction against the soundtrack could force patching or delisting of live titles after Closing. Those costs would fall on Treikaith.

**Recommended fix**
1. Do not rely on the reserved-rights position. In the next APA amendment, negotiate either:
   - an express agreement that Buyer's October 16, 2026 objection is treated as timely for all purposes of §6.3(b); or, preferably,
   - a **special indemnity** for all Losses arising from the Orvenna claim (including re-scoring, patching, delisting and any revenue-share payments), uncapped, with no threshold and recoverable directly from Seller.
2. As a backstop, ask for one or more of:
   - a specific escrow or holdback for the Orvenna claim;
   - a closing condition that the Orvenna claim be resolved or released; and
   - an assignment to Buyer of Seller's indemnity rights against Hallorin Bridge under the Music Composition and License Agreement.
3. Ask Seller now for the current status of the Orvenna demand and any correspondence with Hallorin Bridge.
4. Process point: implement a docketing protocol so that any future Schedule Supplement is calendared and objected to the same day it is received. Objecting by default within the window is costless.

---

### Issue 3: Seller's Kestrune engine license consent is missing from the Required Consents and the closing conditions (HIGH PRIORITY)

**Where it appears**
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.9, Item 3
- Schedule 2.1(c), Item 3
- Schedule 4.5
- APA §§3.2(e), 4.3, 4.5, 6.4, 7.2(d)

**What the documents say**
- **Schedule 4.9, Item 3.** Describes the Kestrune Engine License, the engine, runtime and editor tools on which every Emberfall Saga title and the unreleased sequel build are developed. License §15.3 requires "the prior written consent of Kestrune" for any assignment, including:
  - by operation of law;
  - by merger or change of control; or
  - "in connection with a sale of all or substantially all of the assets of the licensed business."

  Any assignment without consent "is void."
- **Schedule 2.1(c), Item 3.** Lists the license as an Assigned Contract.
- **Schedule 4.5 (Required Consents).** Lists only the Halvern and Ostrava platform consents.
- **APA §7.2(d) and §3.2(e).** Tie the closing condition and Seller's closing deliverable to the consents "set forth on Schedule 4.5." The §6.4 efforts covenant also covers only "Required Consents," which §4.5 defines by reference to Schedule 4.5.
- **Status.** Nothing in the folder shows that Kestrune's consent has been requested or obtained.

**Why it matters for Treikaith**
- This sale is squarely "all or substantially all" of the licensed business. Daibaind's member consent (§1.4) confirms the Purchased Assets are all or substantially all of the company's assets.
- Without consent, the purported assignment is void. Treikaith could close and pay $48,000,000 without a valid license to the engine its entire acquired catalog and sequel pipeline depend on.
- Kestrune would then have leverage to:
  - terminate the license;
  - claim infringement; or
  - demand renegotiated royalties (the current rate is 4.5% of gross revenue above the threshold).
- Treikaith has no closing condition to refuse to close on this basis.
- A claim for breach of the §4.5 or §4.3 consent representations is only a General Representation claim. That claim is:
  - limited to escrow (§9.6);
  - subject to the $240,000 threshold and the Cap; and
  - effectively time-limited to six months (see Issue 4).

  That is a poor remedy for losing the core technology.

**Recommended fix**
1. Require Seller to add the Kestrune consent to Schedule 4.5. This brings it within §§3.2(e), 6.4 and 7.2(d).
2. Separately amend §7.2(d) to name the Kestrune consent expressly, in form reasonably satisfactory to Buyer. The consent should cover the sequel build and future titles, and should confirm there is no royalty increase or consent fee.
3. If Seller cannot obtain consent before the December 31, 2026 outside date, do not waive the condition. Instead, either:
   - negotiate an extension of the outside date; or
   - require a special indemnity plus a holdback for all Losses arising from any failure of the Kestrune license to transfer, recoverable outside the Cap.
4. Ask the client whether Treikaith has its own relationship with Kestrune. A direct license would be a fallback.

---

### Issue 4: The Key Employee Agreement's choice of California law and Los Angeles venue jeopardizes Fenwright's 24-month non-compete (HIGH PRIORITY)

**Where it appears**
- Key Employee Agreement (Treikaith / Lioba Fenwright), §6.1 (Non-Competition) and §9.1 (Governing Law and Venue)
- APA §§6.10, 11.6, 11.7

**What the documents say**
- **APA §6.10.** Requires, as a closing deliverable (§3.2(d)), a Key Employee Agreement with covenants not to compete and not to solicit for **24 months after the Closing Date**. It records that the covenants are necessary to protect the acquired goodwill.
- **Key Employee Agreement §6.1.** Contains that 24-month non-compete. It covers the US, Canada, the UK and the EU, and premium action RPG and fantasy adventure games.
- **Key Employee Agreement §9.1.** Selects "the laws of the State of California" and exclusive venue in "the County of Los Angeles."
- **Mismatch with the APA.** This conflicts with the APA's Delaware law and Chancery forum (§§11.6, 11.7).
- **No precedence clause help.** The APA's precedence clause (§11.10) reaches only Ancillary Agreements "between Buyer and Seller." Fenwright is not Seller, so the precedence clause does not cure the conflict.

**Why it matters for Treikaith**
- California Business and Professions Code §16600 voids contracts that restrain anyone from engaging in a lawful profession, trade or business. Since 2024, §16600.5 also:
  - makes such covenants unenforceable regardless of where or when signed;
  - bars employers from entering into or attempting to enforce them; and
  - gives employees a private right of action with attorneys' fees.
- By choosing California law, Treikaith may be:
  - arguing against its own covenant; and
  - exposing itself to a claim by Fenwright.

  This is so even though she lives and works in Austin (§2.3) and Texas law would generally enforce a reasonable non-compete (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50).
- The sale-of-business exception in Bus. & Prof. Code §16601 may help. Fenwright is a 34% member of Seller (member consent, signature table) and will receive substantial value from the Purchase Price (APA §6.10). But:
  - the covenant sits in an employment agreement with Treikaith, not in a sale instrument signed by her as a selling owner; and
  - the restricted period runs during "the Employment Period" as well as 24 months after Closing.

  The exception is therefore uncertain, and we should not rely on it.
- Treikaith would lose the covenant protecting the creative leadership of the acquired studio, a key piece of the goodwill it is paying for.
- Disputes would be split between Los Angeles and Delaware forums. Los Angeles County is also an odd choice for a San Mateo company with an Austin employee.

**Recommended fix**
1. The agreement appears unsigned, so conform it before Closing. Change §9.1 to Delaware law and Delaware Chancery, consistent with the APA. Texas law and Travis County is an acceptable alternative given her residence and work location.
2. Better still, move the non-compete and non-solicit into a separate **Restrictive Covenant Agreement**:
   - signed by Fenwright in her capacity as a selling equity holder of Daibaind;
   - expressly tied to the sale of goodwill and her share of the Purchase Price; and
   - governed by Delaware law with a Chancery forum.

   Leave the employment terms in the employment agreement.
3. Add express acknowledgments that she:
   - resides and works in Texas; and
   - has not been and will not be primarily employed in California.
4. Add a reasonable-modification (blue-pencil) clause.
5. Make clear that APA §6.10 is not satisfied, and that the §7.2(f) and §3.2(d) closing deliverable is not delivered, unless the agreement contains enforceable restrictive covenants under non-California law.

---

### Issue 5: The six-month escrow release cuts the 18-month survival period for General Representations to six months

**Where it appears**
- APA §9.1 (Survival)
- APA §9.6 (Source of Recovery)
- Escrow Agreement §4.2 (Release Date) and §4.4 (Insufficient Funds)

**What the documents say**
- **APA §9.1.** General Representations survive "until eighteen (18) months after the Closing Date."
- **APA §9.6.** The Indemnity Escrow Funds "then held by the Escrow Agent are the sole and exclusive source of recovery" for breaches of General Representations, Fraud excepted.
- **Escrow Agreement §4.2.** On the date "six (6) months after the Closing Date," the Escrow Agent releases all remaining funds to Seller, less only pending Claim Notices.
- **Escrow Agreement §4.3(a).** Claim Notices may be delivered only "[b]efore the Release Date."
- **Escrow Agreement §4.4.** The Escrow Agent pays nothing beyond funds "then held."
- **APA silence.** The APA itself sets no escrow term.

**Why it matters for Treikaith**
- A General Representation claim first discovered between months 6 and 18 has no source of recovery. The escrow will have been released, and §9.6 bars recovery from Seller directly.
- In practice, the 18-month survival period is six months.
- Many of the risks in this deal surface slowly:
  - royalty and revenue misstatements (§4.4);
  - platform certification and compliance problems after the sequel launches (§4.13);
  - employee IP-assignment gaps (§4.12(d));
  - open-source contamination (§4.12(f));
  - consumer-protection or odds-disclosure compliance (§4.8, given the Texas AG inquiry); and
  - the consent representations (§§4.3, 4.5; see Issue 3).

  Six months is unlikely to be long enough to detect them.
- This interacts with Issue 1. If Excluded Liability claims and the Orvenna claim draw on the same $4.8M escrow early, even less will be available for General Representation claims within the six-month window.

**Recommended fix**
1. In the closing-form Escrow Agreement, move the Release Date in §4.2, and the Claim Notice deadline in §4.3(a), to **18 months after the Closing Date**, aligned with APA §9.1. Before Closing, the Escrow Agreement is still a form (Exhibit D, "substantially in the form").
2. Alternatively, accept a staged release, for example 50% at 12 months and the balance at 18 months, net of pending claims.
3. If Seller insists on six months, amend APA §9.6 so that, after the Release Date, Buyer may recover General Representation Losses directly from Seller up to the Cap.
4. Add a conforming APA amendment stating that the escrow term may not end before the General Representation survival period.

---

### Issue 6: The title representation in APA §4.12(a) covers only registered "Assigned IP," not the source code and unregistered works

**Where it appears**
- APA §4.12(a)
- APA §1.1 (definitions of "Assigned IP" and "Fundamental Representations")
- APA §2.1(b) (definition of "Purchased IP")
- IP Assignment Agreement §1.1 and Exhibit A

**What the documents say**
- **APA §2.1(b).** Conveys "Purchased IP," which expressly includes:
  - all source code, object code, build tools, scripts, pipelines and development tools;
  - all registered **and unregistered** copyrights;
  - art, audio, animation and design assets;
  - unreleased sequel builds and prototypes; and
  - domains and social accounts.
- **APA §4.12(a).** The core title representation, which is a **Fundamental Representation**, says only: "Seller has good and valid title to all **Assigned IP**."
- **APA §1.1.** Gives "Assigned IP" the meaning in the IP Assignment Agreement.
- **IP Assignment Agreement §1.1.** That instrument is a short-form recordation document. It limits Assigned IP to items "registered or applied-for and set forth on Exhibit A," which are four trademarks and two copyright registrations.
- **No precedence clause help.** APA §11.10 does not cure this, because the APA itself adopts the narrower definition.

**Why it matters for Treikaith**
- Seller gives no title warranty for most of the value Treikaith is buying: the code base, the engine-side tooling, the unregistered art and audio, *Tidebreaker* content, and the unreleased sequel build.
- That backing is missing under both the Fundamental Representation (survival to the statute of limitations plus 60 days, with a Cap up to the Purchase Price) and the bring-down at closing (§7.2(a), "true and correct in all respects").
- The remaining IP protections are weaker:
  - §4.12(c) (non-infringement) is knowledge-qualified;
  - §4.12(d) (employee assignments) is a General Representation; and
  - both are escrow-only and, given Issue 5, practically limited to six months.
- The gap matters right now. The Orvenna claim (Issue 2) is a title dispute over unregistered soundtrack works, which is exactly the type of asset §4.12(a) does not reach.

**Recommended fix**
1. Amend APA §4.12(a) to read: "Seller is the sole and exclusive owner of, and has good and valid title to, all **Purchased IP**, free and clear of all Encumbrances other than Permitted Encumbrances." Confirm that §4.12(a) as revised remains a Fundamental Representation.
2. Either delete the cross-reference definition of "Assigned IP" from the APA representations or limit it to the recordation instrument.
3. Leave the IP Assignment Agreement as a short-form recordation instrument. Its narrow definition is appropriate for filing with the USPTO, the Copyright Office and the EUIPO, provided the Bill of Sale or a general IP assignment conveys all Purchased IP.
4. Confirm that the Bill of Sale (not in the folder) expressly conveys all Purchased IP, including unregistered rights and code repositories.

---

## III. Documents Reviewed With No Material Issues

- **Austin Studio Office Lease** (Cottonbluff Properties LP, dated November 2, 2026). This is a Treikaith-only lease and is not a deal document. It contains no APA-related issue.

  One commercial point: the lease commences January 1, 2027 and is not conditioned on Closing. If the APA terminates at the December 31, 2026 outside date, Treikaith keeps a 64-month Austin lease. The client may want to confirm it is comfortable with that.
- **Daibaind Member Consent** (dated September 14, 2026). This appears to be in order. It approves the asset sale by unanimous written consent, as needed for a disposition of all or substantially all of the company's assets.

  It is useful to us in two ways:
  - It confirms that Fenwright is a 34% member who receives value from the sale, which supports the sale-of-business rationale in Issue 4.
  - It confirms that the transaction is a sale of substantially all assets, which supports the Kestrune trigger in Issue 3.

  The Managing Member's authority under ¶3.1(c) covers only Schedule 4.5 consents, so this document should be updated if Kestrune is added.

---

## IV. Recommended Next Steps

1. **Today.** Confirm with the client:
   - whether the October 21 Side Letter was countersigned;
   - the status of the Kestrune consent; and
   - the status of the Orvenna demand.
2. **Prepare Amendment No. 2 to the APA** under §11.9, signed by both parties and expressly stated to be an amendment. It should:
   - restore the Excluded Liabilities carve-out and add a Pre-Closing Player Litigation special indemnity (Issue 1);
   - treat Buyer's October 16 objection as timely and/or add an Orvenna special indemnity (Issue 2);
   - add the Kestrune consent to Schedule 4.5 and §7.2(d) (Issue 3);
   - align the escrow term with the 18-month survival period or permit direct recourse (Issue 5); and
   - expand §4.12(a) to cover all Purchased IP (Issue 6).
3. **Revise the closing-form Escrow Agreement** (§§4.2, 4.3(a)) to match.
4. **Re-paper the Fenwright covenants** under Delaware (or Texas) law before she signs (Issue 4).
5. **Consider the outside date.** Consider whether to propose an extension of the December 31, 2026 outside date so that Treikaith is not pressured to waive the Kestrune or Orvenna protections in order to close.

I am happy to prepare the amendment and the mark-ups on your sign-off.

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Side Letter Removes the Excluded Liabilities Carve-Out from the Cap (IMMEDIATE ATTENTION)

**Where it appears**
- APA §9.5(a)–(b).
- APA §§9.2(c), 2.4(d), 11.9 and 11.10.
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 2.4, Item 1.
- Side Letter §§1.2(a), 2.1, 2.2 and 4.1.

**What the documents say**

As signed, APA §9.5(a) caps Seller's aggregate liability for all Losses under §9.2 at 10% of the Purchase Price ($4,800,000).

APA §9.5(b) removes three categories from the Cap and the threshold:
- (i) Fraud;
- (ii) breach of Fundamental Representations; and
- (iii) "Seller's obligations in respect of Excluded Liabilities pursuant to Section 9.2(c)."

Schedule 2.4, Item 1 lists *Calloway, et al. v. Daibaind Games, LLC* (W.D. Tex. No. 1:26-cv-00814) as an Excluded Liability. This is the putative nationwide consumer class action over the "Ember Cache" randomized purchase mechanics, defined as the "Pre-Closing Player Litigation." Plaintiffs seek restitution, statutory damages, fees and injunctive relief, and the motion to dismiss is still pending.

Side Letter §2.1 "amend[s] and restate[s] in its entirety" §9.5(b). The recitals describe this as a "conforming clarification." The restated text, however, removes the Cap and threshold only for "Fraud or breach of any Fundamental Representation." Clause (iii) is gone.

**Why it matters**

The Side Letter states that it is an amendment executed under §11.9 (Side Letter §4.1). Under §11.10, a §11.9 amendment controls over the APA. Side Letter §2.2 also redirects every reference to §9.5(b) to the restated text.

The result is that Seller's §9.2(c) indemnity for Excluded Liabilities falls back under the general §9.5(a) Cap of $4,800,000. That indemnity covers:
- the player class action and any related or successor actions;
- pre-Closing Taxes; and
- pre-Closing employee liabilities.

The escrow is also only $4.8 million, and it is shared with every other indemnity claim. A nationwide consumer class judgment or settlement, together with defense costs, could easily exceed that amount.

There is a further risk. Plaintiffs may pursue Treikaith as the successor operator of the titles, particularly on the injunctive-relief claims affecting live games it will own. If they do, Treikaith's contractual protection against Seller is capped and practically limited to the escrow.

Nothing in the Side Letter shows that Treikaith received anything in exchange. Calling the change a "conforming clarification" makes it look like a drafting error or an unannounced business change.

**Recommended fix**
- Before Closing, require a further §11.9 amendment that reinstates clause (iii), so that §9.2(c) Losses are again excluded from both the Cap and the threshold.

### Issue 2: Six-Month Escrow Release Undercuts the 18-Month Survival Period (IMMEDIATE ATTENTION)

**Where it appears**
- APA §§9.1 and 9.6.
- Escrow Agreement §§4.2, 4.3(a) and 4.4.

**What the documents say**

APA §9.1 states that General Representations survive "until eighteen (18) months after the Closing Date."

APA §9.6 makes the Indemnity Escrow Funds "then held by the Escrow Agent" the "sole and exclusive source of recovery" for General Representation breaches, except in the case of Fraud.

The APA does not fix the escrow term. Escrow Agreement §4.2 sets the Release Date at "six (6) months after the Closing Date." On that date the Escrow Agent releases all remaining funds to Seller, less the Pending Claim Amount. Escrow Agreement §4.3(a) allows Claim Notices only "[b]efore the Release Date," and §4.4 limits payment to funds then held.

**Why it matters**

Read together, these provisions mean a General Representation claim first asserted between month 6 and month 18 has no source of recovery. The 18-month survival period is effectively six months.

That window is especially short for this business. The problems most likely to appear later include:
- royalty underpayments to Kestrune, which charges 4.5% of gross revenue;
- platform certification or compliance failures after launch (APA §4.13);
- errors in the unaudited financial information (APA §4.4);
- consumer-protection and odds-disclosure compliance (APA §4.8, with the Texas AG inquiry disclosed on Schedule 4.7); and
- contributor IP assignment gaps (APA §4.12(d)).

The APA's precedence clause (§11.10) favors the APA. Even so, it is unclear whether the APA actually conflicts with §4.2, because the APA does not say how long the escrow lasts. We should not rely on §11.10 to fix this.

**Recommended fix**
- Change Escrow Agreement §4.2 so the Release Date is 18 months after the Closing Date, matching APA §9.1.
- As a fallback, allow a partial release (for example, 50%) at 12 months, with the balance held until 18 months.
- Alternatively, or in addition, amend APA §9.6 so that Buyer may recover General Representation Losses directly from Seller, up to the Cap, once the escrow has been released.
- The Escrow Agreement is still in unsigned form. This change should be made before execution at Closing.

### Issue 3: California Law in the Key Employee Agreement Threatens the Fenwright Non-Compete

**Where it appears**
- Key Employee Agreement §§6.1 and 9.1.
- APA §§6.10, 3.2(d), 11.6 and 11.7.

**What the documents say**

APA §6.10 requires, as a closing deliverable, a Key Employee Agreement with 24-month non-compete and non-solicit covenants. The parties acknowledge in §6.10 that these covenants are necessary to protect the acquired goodwill.

Key Employee Agreement §6.1 provides a 24-month non-compete covering the U.S., Canada, the UK and the EU. However, §9.1 selects "the laws of the State of California" and exclusive venue in the state or federal courts in the County of Los Angeles.

Ms. Fenwright lives in Austin and will work there (KEA §2.3). The Key Employee Agreement is between Treikaith and Fenwright rather than between Buyer and Seller. It is therefore not an "Ancillary Agreement" under the APA definition, and the APA's §11.10 precedence clause does not reach it.

**Why it matters**

California Business and Professions Code §16600 voids contracts that restrain anyone from engaging in a lawful profession, trade or business. Under §16600.5, as amended effective 2024, such covenants are unenforceable regardless of where or when the contract was signed, and employees have a private right of action.

By choosing California law, Treikaith has brought in the regime most hostile to its own covenant. California does have a sale-of-business exception (§16601). Its application to Fenwright, a 34% member of Seller, is arguable. But the covenant sits in an employment agreement, runs from Closing rather than from the end of employment, and is drafted as an employment restriction. Relying on that exception carries real litigation risk.

There is also a forum problem. Disputes about the covenant would go to Los Angeles, while APA disputes go to Delaware Chancery. Treikaith could face inconsistent rulings and could lose the injunctive relief it would need quickly (KEA §8.1).

Fenwright is the Studio Creative Director and the creative lead of the franchise. Losing this protection undermines a core reason for the deal.

**Recommended fix**
- Before signing, change KEA §9.1 to Delaware law with Delaware Chancery as the forum, matching the APA. Texas law with Travis County venue is a reasonable alternative, given that Fenwright lives and works in Austin and Texas generally enforces reasonable covenants that are ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement.
- Consider moving the non-compete and non-solicit into a stand-alone restrictive covenant agreement that Fenwright signs in her capacity as a Seller equity holder. That agreement should recite the sale-of-goodwill consideration and be governed by Delaware law, which strengthens the sale-of-business characterization.
- Confirm with Treikaith's employment counsel that California Labor Code §925 does not apply, because Fenwright does not primarily reside or work in California.

### Issue 4: Seller's IP Title Warranty Covers Only Registrations, Not the Source Code

**Where it appears**
- APA §4.12(a), the definition of "Assigned IP" in APA §1.1, and APA §2.1(b).
- IP Assignment Agreement §1.1 and Exhibit A.

**What the documents say**

APA §2.1(b) conveys broadly defined "Purchased IP." That term includes:
- source and object code;
- build tools and pipelines;
- all registered and unregistered copyrights;
- art and audio assets; and
- unreleased sequel builds and prototypes.

The core title representation in APA §4.12(a), however, states only that "Seller has good and valid title to all Assigned IP." The APA defines "Assigned IP" by cross-reference to the IP Assignment Agreement.

IP Assignment Agreement §1.1 limits Assigned IP to items "registered or applied-for and set forth on Exhibit A." Exhibit A lists four trademarks and two copyright registrations, and nothing else.

**Why it matters**

The title warranty, which is also a Fundamental Representation, therefore covers only six registrations. It says nothing about the source code, the unregistered copyrights in the Tidebreaker title and the sequel build, the build tools, or the art and audio assets. Those assets make up most of the value Treikaith is paying for.

The narrower definition affects more than §4.12(a):
- the uncapped Fundamental Representation protection (up to the Purchase Price);
- the long survival period (APA §9.1); and
- the "true and correct in all respects" bring-down condition (APA §7.2(a)).

None of these reach the unregistered assets.

The APA precedence clause does not help, because the APA itself adopts the narrower definition. The other IP representations do not fill the gap:
- §4.12(c) is a knowledge-qualified non-infringement rep; and
- §4.12(d) and §4.12(e) are General Representations, which are subject to the Cap and the escrow problem described in Issue 2.

**Recommended fix**
- Amend APA §4.12(a) to read: "Seller is the sole and exclusive owner of, and has good and valid title to, all Purchased IP, free and clear of all Encumbrances other than Permitted Encumbrances."
- Confirm that the definition of Fundamental Representations continues to capture the revised §4.12(a).
- Keep the IP Assignment Agreement as a short-form recordation instrument. Add to it a general present assignment of all Purchased IP, or deliver a separate omnibus IP assignment at Closing, so that the conveyance of the unregistered assets is documented clearly.

### Issue 5: Kestrune Engine License Consent Is Not a Required Consent or a Closing Condition (IMMEDIATE ATTENTION)

**Where it appears**
- Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.9, Item 3; Schedule 2.1(c), Item 3; and Schedule 4.5.
- APA §§4.3(c), 4.5, 6.4, 3.2(e) and 7.2(d).

**What the documents say**

Schedule 4.9, Item 3 describes the Kestrune Engine License, the engine on which every Emberfall title and the unreleased sequel are built. It quotes Section 15.3 of that license, which bars any assignment without "the prior written consent of Kestrune." The restriction applies "in connection with a sale of all or substantially all of the assets of the licensed business," and any unconsented assignment "is void."

Schedule 2.1(c) lists the license as an Assigned Contract. The member consent confirms that this sale is a disposition of all or substantially all of Seller's assets.

Schedule 4.5 (Required Consents), however, lists only the Halvern and Ostrava platform consents. As a result:
- the §6.4 efforts covenant does not cover Kestrune;
- the §3.2(e) closing deliverable does not cover Kestrune; and
- the §7.2(d) closing condition, which is tied only to consents "set forth on Schedule 4.5," does not cover Kestrune.

Nothing in the folder shows that Kestrune's consent has been requested or obtained.

**Why it matters**

As drafted, Treikaith could be required to close and pay $48 million even though the assignment of the engine license would be void. Without the license, Treikaith could not lawfully keep developing, patching or shipping the Emberfall titles or the sequel on the Kestrune engine.

Kestrune would also gain leverage to renegotiate royalties or demand a consent fee. The APA states that no consent fees are payable for the listed consents and that no party must pay unlisted fees (APA §6.4), so it is unclear who would bear that cost.

Treikaith's after-the-fact remedy is weak. A claim that Schedule 4.5 was incomplete is a claim under the §4.3 and §4.5 General Representations. That claim is capped, limited to the escrow, and subject to the six-month release problem described in Issue 2. Seller may also argue that disclosing the restriction on Schedule 4.9 was enough to qualify §4.3.

**Recommended fix**
- Amend Schedule 4.5 to add Kestrune's written consent to the assignment of the Kestrune Engine License to Treikaith. This will bring it within the §6.4 efforts covenant, the §3.2(e) deliverable and the §7.2(d) closing condition.
- Specify that the consent must be on terms reasonably satisfactory to Buyer, with no change to the royalty rate or scope, and that any consent fee is borne by Seller.
- Ask Seller now for the status of its outreach to Kestrune. Given the December 31, 2026 outside date, we have little time.
- If Seller will not make the consent a closing condition, require an uncapped special indemnity for Losses arising from failure to obtain it, together with a specific holdback.
